name: Center-for-Reproductive-Law-and-Policy-v-Bush_merits_2003-06-16.md
case: Center for Reproductive Law and Policy v. Bush; Second Circuit No. 01-6168; 304 F.3d 183
topology:
Kennedy delivers the opinion of the Court, joined by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer. Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas join the jurisdiction, standing and separate notice holdings; Stone-Zsela also joins the dependent international-law holding. O'Connor files an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Scalia and Thomas. Stone-Zsela files an opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment insofar as it sets aside the speech and equality dismissals.

| Writing or holding | Author | Complete coalition, including author | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jurisdiction, own injuries and notice | Kennedy | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | All nine join. |
| Outside-program speech and equality holdings and mandate | Kennedy | Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Five direct joins; Stone-Zsela supports setting aside dismissal on a distinct rule and remedy. |
| Dependent international-law dismissal | Kennedy | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Six join vacatur and the independent inquiry. |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | O'Connor | O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas | Would affirm speech, equality and the presented duplicative international-law dismissals after finding standing. |
| Partial concurrence and qualified judgment concurrence | Stone-Zsela | Stone-Zsela | Would vacate speech and equality dismissals under strict scrutiny with a justification opportunity; proposes a conditional remedial presumption. |
assignments: **Assignment:** Stone-Zsela assigns Jurisdiction, standing and notice holdings to Kennedy; Stevens assigns Speech and equality holdings and exact mandate to Kennedy; Stone-Zsela assigns International-law disposition to Kennedy. One common author carries the signed lead. Eligible authors: Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer. Balance pool: Stevens, Kennedy, Souter. Kennedy writes the common lead for the component-assigning coalitions. His Rosenberger opinion and actual Velazquez and Southworth joins supply the precise functional distinction between the Government's funded activity and independently financed private expression that the five-Justice holding must articulate. His Bennett and Henderson joins also preserve the concrete domestic injury and operative official-remedy requirements. Stevens's narrow Finley position and Souter's viewpoint and partial-redress analysis are strong alternatives within the pool; Kennedy's demonstrated treatment of governmental attribution offers the particular advantage on the central contested recipient-selection premise. Ginsburg's Velazquez authorship and Breyer's Finley work remain important doctrinal sources but fall outside the fresh pool. Stone assigns the unanimous and international components only; his distinct speech/equality mandate prevents whole-lead eligibility and gives no sixth join to the merits rule. The Chief-governed pool applies to the entire lead, Kennedy is within it, and no artificial part split is made.

name: Georgia-v-Ashcroft_merits_2003-06-26.md
case: Georgia v. Ashcroft, No. 02-182; October Term 2002.
topology:
Stone-Zsela delivered the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer. The complete-opinion coalition is Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas join Part I and the common benchmark, burden, and evidentiary propositions in Part II. O'Connor filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas.

| Opinion portion | Justices adopting it | Exact scope |
|---|---|---|
| Part I | All nine | Live original-plan controversy; continuing intervention dispute; Rule 24 permits and supports the intervention ordered here. |
| Part II: common propositions | All nine | Lawful benchmark comparison; State's ordinary burden; numerical majorities, statewide averages, and legislators' approval are evidence rather than conclusive tests; percentage reduction alone is not retrogression. |
| Part II: effective electoral choice, influence, and application | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Dependable electoral opportunity must be preserved; diffuse influence cannot compensate for its loss; this record supports denial. |
| Part III | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Rejection of the as-applied enforcement-power objection. |
| O'Connor's concurrence in part and dissent | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Would vacate only the original-Senate denial for a broader influence comparison; would reserve the constitutional question. |
